title_en: Calibrating claims and paraphrasing a source

instructions.en: Every item uses the illustrative study summary below, and each item restates the facts it needs. Two skills are practised. Calibration: a claim should be exactly as strong as its evidence, so over-claiming and stacking hedges are both errors. Paraphrase: restating a source in your own words and your own sentence structure, with attribution. Keeping the source's structure and swapping some words (patchwriting) is a normal stage in learning to write from sources, not a sign of dishonesty; the fix is to understand the idea, look away from the source, and rebuild the sentence.

input_text:
Illustrative source (invented for this task: the authors, the journal, the town and all figures are fictional).

Ferrant, L., & Oyelaran, T. (2024). Planted roofs and summer indoor temperatures in Marrowby: a one-summer comparison. Marrowby Urban Review, 3(2), 14-29.

Summary: During one summer in the town of Marrowby, the researchers compared 12 apartment buildings with planted (green) roofs and 12 similar buildings with ordinary roofs. On the hottest days, top-floor apartments under planted roofs were on average 1.5 °C cooler in the afternoon than those under ordinary roofs. The difference was smaller on lower floors and almost disappeared on the ground floor. The authors note that the buildings were not randomly assigned, that the planted-roof buildings were on average newer, and that one summer may not be typical. They conclude that planted roofs "may help to reduce indoor heat on upper floors" and call for a study over several years.

scaffold.en: Calibrate to the evidence: large, repeated or controlled studies support "shows" and "demonstrates"; one small, non-randomised study supports "suggests", "indicates" and "may".

Hedging phrase bank by function: distancing ("It has been suggested that..."), cautious interpretation ("These results suggest that..."), avoiding over-generalisation ("on upper floors", "in this sample", "generally").
Paraphrase in four steps: read until you understand, look away, write the idea in your own structure, then check the meaning against the source and add the citation.

checklist.en: My claims are as strong as the evidence: no "proves" or "all" for one small study, and no pile of hedges either.
I hedge once for each job (a reporting verb such as "suggests" for limited evidence, a modal such as "may" for a possible effect), never stack hedges that do the same job, and keep the scope precise.
My paraphrase changes both the words and the sentence structure, keeps the meaning, and names the source.
I quote only when the exact wording matters, and I attribute every idea that comes from a source.

items.question: A fictional study compared 12 planted-roof and 12 ordinary-roof buildings in one town over one summer; the buildings were not randomly assigned, and top-floor flats under planted roofs were on average 1.5 °C cooler on the hottest afternoons. Which sentence reports this with the right strength?
options: Green roofs keep buildings cool in summer, so every new apartment building should have one.
This study proves that green roofs lower indoor temperatures, and the same result can be expected in every city.
This small, non-randomised study suggests that planted roofs may reduce heat in top-floor flats on the hottest days.
It could perhaps be possible that green roofs might possibly have some kind of effect on temperature in certain cases.

0.en: Over-claimed: no scope (which floors? which days?), a possible effect stated as a general fact, and a policy drawn from one small study.

1.en: Over-claimed: one town and one summer cannot prove anything about every city.

3.en: Over-hedged: so many hedges that the reader cannot tell what was found.

explanation.en: Calibration means scope plus strength. The calibrated sentence keeps the scope (top-floor flats, hottest days), flags the design limit (small, non-randomised), and hedges the interpretation ("suggests", "may").

prompt.en: Each sentence describes the fictional green-roof study (24 buildings, one town, one summer, not randomised; top-floor flats under planted roofs were on average 1.5 °C cooler on the hottest afternoons). Sort the sentences.

items.text: Planted roofs eliminate summer heat in apartment buildings.
The study shows beyond doubt that every city should require planted roofs.
On the hottest afternoons, top-floor flats under planted roofs were on average 1.5 °C cooler.
The authors suggest that planted roofs may reduce indoor heat on upper floors.
It might perhaps be possible that planted roofs could possibly have some effect.
There may possibly be some slight indication that top floors could perhaps be somewhat cooler.

explanation.en: A reported observation needs no hedge when its scope is stated (top floors, hottest afternoons, on average). An interpretation needs one. "Eliminate" and "beyond doubt" claim more than 24 buildings in one summer can show, while four hedges in one clause claim almost nothing.

prompt.en: Calibrate the claim about the fictional one-summer, 24-building study. Choose from the bank.

items.text: This study ___ that planted roofs ___ reduce heat in top-floor flats on very hot days.

feedback.en: One non-randomised summer cannot prove a general claim. Use a verb that reports evidence without certainty.
Nothing about a small, one-summer comparison is beyond doubt.
"Always" claims more than the study measured: it found an average difference on the hottest afternoons.
"Will definitely" turns a possible effect into a certain one.

explanation.en: The reporting verb and the modal do different jobs: "suggests" marks the evidence as limited, and "may" marks the effect as possible. Two hedges with different jobs are normal academic usage; four in one clause, all doing the same job, are not.

prompt.en: This sentence stacks four hedges that all do the same job. Rewrite it so that the single modal "may" carries the uncertainty: start with "Planted roofs may" and keep the verb "reduce".

items.source: It might perhaps be possible that planted roofs could possibly reduce heat on upper floors.
answers: Planted roofs may reduce heat on upper floors.
Planted roofs may reduce heat on the upper floors.

wrong_feedback.match: Planted roofs may possibly reduce heat on upper floors.

feedback.en: Still two hedges doing the same job: "may" already marks the possibility, so "possibly" adds nothing.

wrong_feedback.match: Planted roofs may help to reduce heat on upper floors.

feedback.en: "May help to reduce" is a well-calibrated phrase (the authors use it), but here the task is to cut hedges, not to add a new softener. Keep the verb "reduce" and let "may" alone carry the uncertainty.

explanation.en: "Might", "perhaps", "possible" and "could possibly" all mark the same uncertainty. One modal is enough, and the scope ("on upper floors") keeps the claim precise.

items.question: Source sentence (fictional study, Ferrant & Oyelaran, 2024): "On the hottest days, top-floor apartments under planted roofs were on average 1.5 °C cooler in the afternoon than those under ordinary roofs." Which version is an acceptable paraphrase?
options: On the hottest days of the summer, top-floor flats under green roofs were on average 1.5 °C cooler in the afternoon than those under normal roofs (Ferrant & Oyelaran, 2024).
Ferrant and Oyelaran (2024) report that, on the hottest days, afternoon temperatures in top-floor flats beneath green roofs averaged 1.5 °C lower than in comparable flats beneath conventional roofs.
Planted roofs make top-floor apartments 1.5 °C cooler in the afternoon, which shows how effective they are on hot days.
Top-floor apartments under planted roofs were on average 1.5 °C cooler in the afternoon than those under ordinary roofs on the hottest days of summer.

0.en: Patchwriting: the source's structure with a few words swapped. It is cited, but it is not yet your own sentence. Look away from the source and rebuild it.

2.en: No attribution, and the scope has slipped ("on average" and "the hottest days" are gone), so the claim over-generalises.

3.en: The source's own words, reshuffled, with no attribution. Rebuild the sentence from the idea, and cite it.

explanation.en: A paraphrase keeps the meaning (including the figure and its scope), changes the wording and the sentence structure, and names the source. Patchwriting is a normal step on the way; to move past it, write the idea from memory, then check the meaning and add the citation.

prompt.en: Source sentence (fictional study, Ferrant & Oyelaran, 2024): "The difference was smaller on lower floors and almost disappeared on the ground floor." Sort each version.

items.text: The difference was smaller on the lower floors and nearly vanished on the ground floor (Ferrant & Oyelaran, 2024).
The gap was smaller on lower storeys and almost disappeared at street level (Ferrant & Oyelaran, 2024).
Ferrant and Oyelaran (2024) found that the cooling effect weakened on the lower floors until it was barely measurable at ground level.
According to Ferrant and Oyelaran (2024), the benefit was concentrated on the upper storeys and was close to zero on the ground floor.
The cooling effect weakened on the lower floors until it was barely measurable at ground level.
Lower floors gained less from the planted roofs, and ground-floor flats gained almost nothing.

explanation.en: Patchwriting keeps the source's skeleton ("the difference was smaller on X and almost disappeared on Y") and swaps words. A paraphrase rebuilds the sentence around the idea. Either way, an idea from a source needs a citation, even when every word is your own.

prompt.en: Choose the reporting verb that represents the source fairly.

items.question: The fictional authors conclude, cautiously, that planted roofs "may help to reduce indoor heat on upper floors". Complete: "Ferrant and Oyelaran (2024) ___ that planted roofs may help to reduce indoor heat on upper floors."

0.en: This makes the authors sound far more certain than they are.

2.en: This makes the authors sound far more certain than they are.

explanation.en: Reporting verbs carry stance. "Suggest" matches tentative authors; "prove" or "establish beyond doubt" would misrepresent the source by making it sound more certain than it is.

items.question: When you write about the fictional green-roof study, when is it better to quote the authors' exact words than to paraphrase them?
options: When the wording itself matters, such as the authors' cautious claim that planted roofs "may help to reduce indoor heat".
Whenever a sentence is difficult to paraphrase, because quoting saves you from working out exactly what it means.
For every sentence you take from the study, because quoting is always safer and more accurate than paraphrasing.
Never: academic writing avoids direct quotation and expects every idea from a source to be paraphrased.

explanation.en: Quote when the wording itself is the evidence, such as a hedged conclusion whose caution you want to show. Otherwise paraphrase or summarise. Quotation, paraphrase and summary all need attribution.
